item.title: Chemistry Seminar Presented by Prof. Peter Mahaffy (The King’s University, Edmonton) Realizing the Role for Chemistry and Chemistry Education in the Emergence of Sustainability: A Systems Approach — Tue Nov 3, 11:40 AM — French Family Science Center 2237
item.description:
The Department of Chemistry is excited to host Prof. Peter Mahaffy (The King's University, Edmonton) on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, for a departmental seminar.
The sustainability challenges facing our planet are so pressing that they require urgent attention by science through a convergence of disciplinary approaches. Chemistry, the science of transformation of matter, has a central role to play in addressing the unintended consequences that arise from the large-scale material transformation by humans over the past fifty years. How can we fully realize chemistry's role in the emergence of sustainability, beginning with the molecular basis of sustainability and integrating sustainability orientations, tools, and frameworks into the practice of chemistry and chemistry education? item.title: Sow What? Growing Native Plants from Seed (Online) — Thu Nov 5, 7:00 PM
item.description: Join NCWF South Wake Conservationists Chapter for a webinar about native seed sowing! Native plant propagation is a way to restore ecological relationships, strengthen local seed systems, and cultivate resilient communities. This talk explores the art and science of growing native plants from seed, from the fundamentals of seed stratification and substrate selection, to accessible, low-tech propagation methods that anyone can try at home or in their community. We will examine the native seed supply chain and the importance of species availability, regional ecotypes, and genetic diversity in supporting the specialized relationships between native plants, pollinators, and other wildlife. Moving from backyard experiments to large-scale production, we’ll also explore advanced propagation techniques and how they are implemented at a native wetland plant nursery. Finally, we’ll consider the potential of native food crops to bridge communities passionate about biodiversity, sustainable food

The islands of Lake Norman provide critical refuge for all kinds of wildlife including deer, fish, songbirds, raptors and pollinators. Native buttonbushes reduce erosion and stabilize island shorelines, while increasing habitat and forage for waterfowl, pollinators, and other wildlife. Volunteers are needed to install brown-headed nuthatch nest boxes and plant the hundreds of buttonbushes across several islands. We will meet at Safe Harbor Skippers Landing where the islands are a short boat ride away. We will provide all boats and tools. Please bring water and gloves, and come dressed in layers. We strongly recommend knee-high waterproof boots or waders. Pizza and drinks will be provided to all volunteers at the end.

item.title: Save Our Sounds: Standing Up for NC's Marine Habitats, Fish Populations, and Public Recreation (Chapel Hill and Online)) — Mon Nov 16, 6:30 PM
item.description:
Did you know North Carolina’s sounds are the second largest in the U.S. and serve as a vital nursery for sea life which populates the entire eastern seaboard? Unfortunately, North Carolina marine fisheries management has allowed fishing practices that for decades have failed to protect our fish populations (especially juveniles), other sea life, and our sea floor. Join NCWF Tri-County Conservationists Chapter and Ann Berry Somers for an eye-opening talk on why our shallow sounds are in deep trouble and learn about the Save Our Sounds campaign. Discover what’s at stake for our ecosystems, anglers, and the economies of our coastal communities—and learn how we can demand better stewardship together. REGISTER HERE
Source: NC Wildlife Federation

Created by Olivia Aston Bosworth and Samantha Provenzano Commissioned by Alliance Theatre Originally developed and produced by the Alliance Theatre (Atlanta, GA) as part of the Kathy and Ken Bernhardt Theatre for the Very Young series. item.title: Great Coharie River Tree Tour (Clinton) — Sat Nov 21, 9:30 AM
item.description:
Join NCWF and the Alliance for Cape Fear Trees for a guided tour of the Great Coharie River. Once logged extensively, the Coharie River still has many large swamp chestnut oaks, pine, and bald cypress trees. The tour includes beaver dams, winding blackwater channels, and a tour of the Coharie tribal center with a 650-year-old dugout canoe. Come for the trees and leave with a deeper understanding of indigenous ecological stewardship. Ages 13+ REGISTER HERE
Source: NC Wildlife Federation
